name: The Cinderblock Biennale (Shelf Gallery Circuit)
description: Every eighteen months since 2211, an anonymous coordination body known only as the Frame sends simultaneous activation signals to dozens of pre-staged installation sites across Shelf territory — abandoned storefronts, drainage culverts, the interiors of derelict transit cars — converting them overnight into a sprawling, walkable gallery that exists for exactly seventy-two hours before vanishing. Works range from massive ferrocrete sculpture to bioluminescent living murals grown from modified fungal cultures, and participating artists are forbidden from signing their pieces. The Biennale is explicitly anti-market: no works are for sale, no BCI capture of the installations is permitted (though enforcement is social rather than technical), and documentation exists only in people's memories and illegal stills. The 2217 iteration, which incorporated the ruins of the Halverson-Cheng processing plant, drew an estimated twelve thousand visitors including several Tier 4 and Tier 5 attendees who arrived in unmarked vehicles.
cultural_impact: The Biennale has become a rare site of genuine cross-tier cultural pilgrimage, and its anti-documentation ethic has spawned a broader 'presence-only' art philosophy that has influenced even some sanctioned Tier 3 galleries.
key_figures: Adesola Brennan-Kozlov (art critic, documented three iterations)
locations: Halverson-Cheng ruins, South Shelf industrial zone
Shelf transit car graveyard, Depot Row
story_hooks: A Tier 5 corponation executive wants to acquire and legitimize the Biennale brand; the Frame is considering a response that goes beyond refusal.
One of the 2220 installations contains information — encoded in the work itself — that someone powerful wants suppressed before the seventy-two hours are up.
A participant discovers that one piece in the current Biennale is not art but a functional device, and no one knows who placed it or why.
